MI Farooqui with M Saleemullah, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner.

parties:
Bakth Bibi ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Government of Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Mohammad Gholam Rabbani, J.: This application under Article 102 of the Constitution is directed against the judgment and order dated 7.3.89 passed by the Court of Settlement in Case No. 1022 of 1987. The case was filed by the petitioner Bakht Bibi for the release of a three storied building at 93 Chatteswary Road, Chittagong, from the list of the abandoned property declared abandoned and taken possession by the Government under the President's Order No. 16 of 1972. By the impugned judgment and order the Court of Settlement dismissed the case. 

 In 1955 the petitioner came to Chittagong with her father from Afghanistan without passport. In 1961 she was married to Abdul Khaleq another national of Afghanistan residing at Chittagong and in time out of this wed-lock she gave birth to five children—two sons and three daughters. The said house property is known as Kabliwala Building which was constructed by her husband on the land purchased partly in the name of her husband and partly in her name by two registered sale deeds respectively dated 19.12.58 and 1.6.67. During the war of liberation her husband died. Thereafter she left this country for Afghanistan with her daughters leaving at Chittagong her two minor sons in the house of her maternal uncle Chunnu Mia a Peon in the local Custom Office. Subsequently in 1981 she came back to Chittagong with Afghanistani passport and made representations to the authority concerned for the release of her said house property; but in vain. Ultimately she filed the aforesaid case before the Court of Settlement stating that she being a national of Afghanistan, her said property did not come under the category of the abandoned property as defined in President's Order No. 16 of 1972. 

 3. The Government contested the case alleging that the petitioner was an imposter and not the widow of late Abdul Khaleqe. Both Abdul Khaleq and the petitioner were nationals of Pakistan. As the house property in question was left uncared for and the whereabouts of Abdul Khaleq was unknown to the Government, the same was rightly declared as abandoned property and was taken under the control and management of the Government. 

 6. The second ground, in the language of the Court of Settlement, "the case holding cannot be identified at all with reference to the alleged purchase deeds of Abdul Khaleq and Bakth Bibi noted above, showing their right and interest in the case holding" is also not sustainable. This ground, a third case, was invented by the Court of Settlement. The Government did neither challenge the indentity of the property in question vis-a-vis the sale deeds—nor the title of Abdul Khaleq or Bakht Bibi to the property in question. The case of the Government is that the petitioner was not the wife of Abdul Khaleq and as such she did not inherit the same. The Government, however, failed to challenge the claim of the petitioner that a portion of the land was purchased in her name and the Court of Settlement equally failed to notice this unchallenged fact. 

 8. Fourth ground, to quote from the impugned judgment, "it is very curious that petitioner claims the case holding by way of alleged purchase as per sale deed dated 6.5.67 noted above and at the same breath she has made her two sons Md. Nadir and Md. Amanullah petitioners in this case holding claiming interest in the case holding, but it is contradictory as two sons has no locus standi so long as the petitioner No. 1 is alive"-is also not sustainable. As already stated the land on which the building in question stands was purchased by two sale deeds, one in the name of the petitioner and the other in the name of Abdul Khaleque and as such petitioner's two sons also inherited a portion of the said property after the death of their father Abdul Khaleque. 

 9. The fifth ground, to quote, "It cannot be held that Abdul Khaleque is now dead. It is all the more curious that the petitioner in her petition dated 13.4.85 addressed to DC Chittagong, does not assert as to the death of her alleged husband Abdul Khaleque in 1971" is not sustainable. While deposing before the Court of Settlement the petitioner stated in her cross-examination that she had filed the death certificate of her father and husband but she was not further cross-examine challenging the genuineness of these certificates. The fifth ground that the petitioner is a Pakistan national according to her own showing in her alleged Kabala dated 5.6.67 is a queer finding of the Court of Settlement. In 1967 if the petitioner described herself as a Pakistani that does not mean that she remained a Pakistani for all time to come. Such a causal description of the citizenship of the purchaser in the sale deed written by a deed-writer cannot be basis for determining the citizenship of the purchaser. Moreover, the conduct of her husband indicates otherwise. We find from the record that as early as in 1963 her husband Abdul Khaleque applied for the citizenship of Pakistan but his prayer was rejected holding that he was still an Afghan national. Apart from that, the petitioner is a national of Afghanistan in view of the passport issued by the Democratic Republic of Afghanistan and this fact was not denied by the respondent Government. 

 11. Last ground is that since admittedly the petitioner left Bangladesh before the war of liberation, leaving the property uncared for and her where about was unknown, the property was rightly declared as abandoned property. This finding is also erroneous. According to Article 2(1) of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 for the purpose of this Writ Petition, abandoned property means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, "including" any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh, but does not include" any property the owner of which is residing outside of Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh". 

 12. We hold that the petitioner is not a citizen of Pakistan but is a citizen of Afghanistan which was not at war with Bangladesh and as such her property cannot come under the category of "including" and her property comes under the category of "does not include" as the Government does not say that the purpose of her residing outside Bangladesh was prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. 

 14. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. It is declared that the judgment and order dated 7.3.89 being annexure 'J' to this writ petition passed by the Court of Settlement in Case No. 1022 of 1987 are declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and be of no legal effect. It is ordered that the house property at 93 Chatteswari, Chittagong, be excluded from the list of abandoned property and its vacant possession be given to the petitioner within three months from date. 

 17. It is an undisputed fact that after coming into force of President's Order No. 16 of 1972  i.e. the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 the Government treated this property as abandoned property as defined in Article of the said President's Order and took over possession of the property by applying section 7 of the said President’s Order No. 16 of 1972. It is also undisputed that this property was listed as abandoned property in the 'Ka' list by Notification in the Official Gazette on September 23, 1986 (Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary) at page No. 9762 (102) against Serial No. 84 under the provisions of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 and it is also undisputed that in order to release the said property from the list of abandoned property as published vide the aforesaid notification in the gazette the petitioner filed an application in the Court of the Settlement which was registered as Case No. 1022 of 1987 and that the Court of Settlement dismissed the petition vide judgment and order dated 7.3.89 and affirmed the decision of the Government to treat this property as abandoned properly. As against the aforesaid decision of the Government to treat; the disputed house as abandoned property and the decision of the Court of Settlement affirming the aforesaid decision of the Government that the petitioner filed this Writ Petition before this court in its writ jurisdiction and obtained the present Rule. In order to ascertain whether the disputed house in question was "abandoned property" it is necessary to refer to Article 2 of the Presidents Order No. 16 of 1972, Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 which runs as follows: 

 (1) "abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property  including. 

 (i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh; 

 (ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972), but does not include- 

 (a) any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh; 

 (b) any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force. 

 (5) "Property" means property of any kind, movable or immovable and includes any right or interest in such property and any debt or actionable claim, any security or negotiable instrument, any right under a contract and any industrial or commercial undertaking; 

 18. The definition of abandoned property appearing in Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 was dealt with in a number of cases by the Appellate Division of this Court and also High Court Division of this Court The earliest of these cases relied upon by Mr. Farooqui, the learned Advocate for the petitioner; is M/s ATJ Industries Limited and others Vs. The Government of Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR page 27. The meaning of "abandoned property" appearing in Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972 has been elaborately dealt with and interpreted in this case. 'In subsequent cases also the meaning of "abandoned property" came up for consideration and in this connection, Mr. Farooqui placed reliance on 28 DLR (AD) 120 which arose out of the same case decided by the High Court Division and reported in 28 DLR 27. The last of the cases relied upon by Mr. Farooqui is Government of Bangladesh Vs. MS Ispahani reported in 40 DLR 116 in which Mr. Badrul Haider Chowdhury J. as his Lordship was then, traced the history of the gradual development of interpretation of "abandoned property" appearing in Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972. The principle that has been settled in these cases culminating in Ispahani's case is that clause of Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972 has two inclusion sub-clauses being sub-clauses (i) and (ii) and also two exclusion, sub-clauses appearing as sub-clauses (a) and (b) thereof. It was laid down in this case that inclusion clauses (i) and (ii) are independent of the main clause (1) and it was also held in this case that exclusion clauses (a) and (b) qualify the main clause (1). We are however, not concerned with the exclusion sub-clause (b) as it is nobody's case that the disputed house was controlled and possessed by the Government under any law for the time being in force. We are mainly concerned with the exclusion sub-clause sub-clause (a). It is an undisputed fact that the disputed house was treated as abandoned property not by operation of inclusion sub-clause (i) or inclusion sub-clause (ii) but by operation of the main clause (1) which provided that a property would be deemed to be abandoned property if the person owning the said property was not present in Bangladesh or if his whereabouts were not known or if he had ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property. The Government appears to have applied this main clause (1) in treating the disputed house as abandoned property on the ground that the owner of the disputed house was not present in Bangladesh and that his whereabouts were not known and that he had ceased to occupy supervise or manage in person said property. The Government could have treated this property as abandoned property if the condition in only anyone of the three sub-clauses of clause (1) of Article 2 was present as all these three sub-clauses were held to be disjunctive and not conjunctive. It was also held in this case that while applying the exclusion clause (a) what was to be seen in the case of a person residing outside Bangladesh was whether he was residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, was prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh, before treating his property as abandoned property and if the answer was in the affirmative the property was to be deemed to be abandoned property. The crux of the principle was that the Government has to form an opinion as to whether the residence of the person outside of Bangladesh was a purpose prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh or not. It was not, however, argued in this case whether this exclusion clause (a) qualifies the entire main clause (1) of Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972 and Mr. Farooqui advanced considerable argument on this point contending that the exclusion clause (a) qualifies the main clause (1) of Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972. We have carefully perused the main clause (1) along with the exclusion (a) of Article 2 of the above President's Order and it appears to us that the main clause (1) has three parts consisting of the following: 

 (3) "who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property". 

 It appears that there three parts together constituted the entire sentence appearing in clause (1). The exclusion clause (a) does not specifically mention that it qualified only one of the above parts appearing in the main clause (1). So, it appears to us that exclusion (a) qualifies the entire paragraph consisting of the three above parts appearing in clause (1). 

 19. Since, we have held that exclusion clause (a) is an exception to the entire main paragraph appearing in clause (1) of Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972, it has now to be decided whether the petitioner was entitled to get when the petitioner was out of the territory of Bangladesh when PO 16 of 1972 came into force on 28th February, 1972. There is nothing on record to show either before this court or before the Court of Settlement that the residence of the petitioner outside Bangladesh was for a purpose prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh and, as such, following the principles laid down in the aforesaid cases culminating in Government of Bangladesh Vs. M/s. Ispahani reported in 40 DLR 116 we are of opinion that without forming an opinion that the petitioner stayed outside Bangladesh for a purpose which was prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh the Government could not treat the disputed house as abandoned property. Since the stay of the petitioner outside the territory of Bangladesh prior to on or after the date of promulgation of PO 16 of 1972 had not been proved to be prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh she ought to have been excluded from the operation of clause (4) of Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972 and as such, her property i.e. the disputed house was not at all abandoned property within the definition of clause (1) of Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972. In the above view of the matter, we are of the opinion that the treatment of the property and listing of the said property as abandoned property in the 'Ka' list in Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary at page No. 8762 (102) against Serial No. 84 dated September 23, 1985 and the decision of the Court of Settlement dated 7.3.89 in 1022 of 1987 affirming the above action of the Government are without authority and of no legal effect. I, therefore, agree with the order proposed to be passed by my learned brother.
